radicals.meaningMnemonic: This looks like a <radical>hook</radical>, like the kind a pirate would wear. The flat line shows where the hand was cut off, and the hook is right above, ready to take its place. Yarrrr.

This is the <radical>snake</radical> radical. See the head at the top with its long skinny body stretching down from it?

Don't confuse this with 己 (oneself) — the snake has an extra line behind its head to connect to the rest of its body.

This is the radical for <radical>cloud</radical>. See how the cloud is puffy on the bottom but has two lines up top? That's because a plane flew through it.

It was a nice cloud to hang out privately in, until that darn plane came through and ruined it. So much for your private cloud!

Stick a table on top of a stool and you end up with a very dangerous <radical>weapon</radical>. Imagine hitting someone with this thing! Or, even better, imagine making someone sit on it. They'd be crushed mentally and emotionally and whatnot. Now that's a scary weapon.

This radical is made up of two slightly different versions of the spoon radical. Look closely at these two spoons. <radical>Compare</radical> their differences, like the different angles in the bends of the spoons. It's like one of those "spot the difference" games where you compare two similar pictures. But this time it's with spoons.
This is a <radical>net</radical>, spread out over the water. Imagine all the fish you can catch in this net!

Most of this radical is just the rice radical, but the top part is something coming to cut the rice from its stalk. That, my friend, is the <radical>sickle</radical>. See how the rice is still there? That's because it's in motion. The sickle is literally doing the cutting RIGHT NOW! (And don't confuse this with the grain 禾 radical!)

This radical looks like a <radical>horse</radical>. See the long, thick neck with the mane flowing to the right? What might look like a wing is actually the horse's four legs and its tail hanging down.

Don't confuse this radical with the bird radical (鳥). They look similar, but this one doesn't have the little feather sticking out of the top of its head!
Flying to the sun with wings is <radical>easy</radical>! Or so Icarus thinks. Someone should probably tell him…

You find a coffin on the sun. It's burnt to a crisp from the heat, but there's definitely someone in there. You wonder who this mysterious someone might have been. Whoever they were, they got a fancy sun burial, so they really must've been someone (or shall we say, sun-one?).

This is the radical for <radical>suit</radical>, like when something suits you. You find a hat on the ground, and when you pick it up, there's a mouth underneath. "It suits you! It suits you!" the mouth says. You try the hat on, and yup — it really suits! It's weird getting fashion advice from a random mouth, but hey, it wasn't wrong.

This radical is a <radical>cage</radical> because it's covered on all sides but one (the one open side is where the cage door or gate is). There's nothing inside this cage because there's no gate, and whatever was inside has gotten out. I hope it wasn't rabid...

This looks like the kind of building you'd find in a Japanese <radical>capital</radical>. See the ornate roof and the stone foundation flaring out underneath, like a castle? The emperor lives in there. And wherever the emperor lives automatically becomes the capital city. That's why this radical is capital.

Alternatively, you can use the radical parts and imagine a giant lid on the pot that will feed the mouths of all the small people in the capital.

This is a <radical>cape</radical>, like the kind a superhero would wear. Use your imagination to picture a hero facing left, with a cape tied around their neck and hanging down their back. With that cape on, they're ready to save the world!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The poor <radical>alligator</radical> was taken far inland by a <radical>tsunami</radical>. Now his only source of water is a tiny <kanji>pond</kanji> that barely fits his body, and doesn't even provide much food.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine the alligator riding the tsunami in. When he hits the ground, and the water recedes, he's all alone in a pond, but it doesn't provide much for him. Imagine him looking for food in the little, shallow pond. Imagine him trying to stay wet... it's just not a great situation to be in, unfortunately.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The worst part about this <kanji>pond</kanji> is that the only thing for the alligator to eat is <reading>chee</reading>se (ち). Cheese may be yummy for humans, but alligators hate it. They'd rather eat the cow the cheese came from. Sadly, this pond is full of cheese.
kanji.readingHint: Picture an alligator crying in a pond full of cheese. It's eating a piece really slowly and weeping.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Ice</radical> is what you're <radical>lack</radical>ing, so the <kanji>next</kanji> thing you need to do is go to the store and see if they have any. Nope, no ice. So, now you go to the next store. Is there ice here? Nope. Next!
kanji.meaningHint: Feel a little frustrated you can't find ice. Have the words "<kanji>next</kanji> next next" echoing through your head as you go from store to store, irritated.
kanji.readingMnemonic: To remember the reading じ, we used the word "Jesus" - Finally, when you're at the last store in existence, you decide it's time to pray to <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ), asking for a miracle. He comes down from the heavens with ice in his hands.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine him coming down. Imagine your surprise. He hands you the ice, and it's cold. You thank him, and he flies away.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Just like the radical, the kanji means <kanji>capital</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Know your radicals!
kanji.readingMnemonic: To remember the reading きょう we use the old <kanji>capital</kanji> of Japan, Kyoto, which is spelled <reading>きょう</reading>と. It was the capital of Japan before Tokyo!
kanji.readingHint: When you think of the capital, any capital, think of きょうと.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>branch</radical> radical and the <kanji>branch</kanji> kanji are the same! This kanji also means <kanji>support</kanji>. To remember it, think about a tree with lots of branches. The branches support each other and the trunk of the tree. If you were to climb the tree, the branches would be able to support your weight too!
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a branch supporting the weight of you, your entire family, and maybe a few friends.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You're happily sitting on this <kanji>branch</kanji>, letting it <kanji>support</kanji> all this weight, when a <reading>shee</reading>p (し) starts to climb the tree. A very, very big sheep. Uh oh... no no, sheep. If you get on this branch it won't be able to support all this weight!!!
kanji.readingHint:
The big sheep walks up the side of the tree with its weird hooves and starts to put its weight on the branch. "No no no!" you and your whole family scream. The branch can't support the weight of the sheep. It snaps! You all tumble to the ground.

The end.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> of the <radical>master</radical>s gets to choose the place they <kanji>dwell</kanji>. So they <kanji>reside</kanji> in a huge mansion on the top of the mountain, surrounded by all the other masters in their smaller dwellings.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture the leader master who dwells in a big, beautiful dwelling. Everyone else is jealous.
kanji.readingMnemonic: She needs this big place to <kanji>dwell</kanji> so she has somewhere to store all of her <reading>jew</reading>els (じゅう). Masters always have lots of fancy, expensive things, and she has jewels.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine opening the door to the leader master's dwelling and thousands of jewels come pouring out, whisking you off, down the mountain.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: With <radical>top hat</radical> <radical>power</radical>, you're able to <kanji>help</kanji> anyone.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine putting on your top hat and getting power from it. Then, you use that power to help someone. It's important to make the association that it's the top hat giving you the power to help that person. You're basically Frosty the Snow Man.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The person you <kanji>help</kanji> with your top hat power? It's <reading>Jo</reading>-Anne (じょ).
kanji.readingHint:
You can imagine saving her however you like. Perhaps she was under a car, and you used your top hat powers to help her out of that situation by lifting it above your head.

Note: Jo-Anne is the character we're using with じょ reading mnemonics. She is short compared to Joe (じょう), the giant farmhand, which is how you'll differentiate the two similar readings.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You're in a <radical>cage</radical> and you've been shot by an <radical>arrow</radical>. Obviously things are looking pretty bad. You need some <kanji>medicine</kanji> if you hope to live.
kanji.meaningHint: More specifically, antibiotics. Your wound is festering pretty badly.
kanji.readingMnemonic:
When we need to remember the sound い we use the word "Eagle."

You need your <kanji>medicine</kanji> really bad. Then, you look up. There's an <reading>ea</reading>gle (い) flying overhead. He has a package. It's medicine! You're saved!
kanji.readingHint: Or, so you think. He just keeps circling and circling. Feel some hate for the eagle. Why isn't he dropping the medicine? You don't have long to live!

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
<radical>Wolverine</radical> is going down a <radical>slide</radical> and from your <radical>mouth</radical> you scream, "Hey, <kanji>buddy</kanji>! Watch it with that slide, it's really fast and you might hurt yourself, buddy!" 

You're a really good buddy to Wolverine. He also happens to be the local <kanji>ruler</kanji> of these lands. You make it a habit to befriend the local strongmen, just in case… No wonder you're so buddy-buddy with all the rulers around here.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine having all the local rulers as your buddies, all the influence you would have. You might end up with everyone wanting to be your buddy.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The biggest perk of having Wolverine as your <kanji>buddy</kanji> is that he teaches you <reading>kun</reading>g fu (くん). Wolverine wants you, his good buddy, to know how to defend yourself. That's why he uses his martial arts knowledge to train you in kung fu every day after he gets done playing on the slide.
kanji.readingHint: There's no better way to bond with a good buddy than some daily kung fu sparring.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Writing</radical> and <radical>measurement</radical> stand <kanji>versus</kanji> one another. Writing is all about feeling and expression. Measurement is about cold hard numbers. Yep, in this world writing people are basically the <kanji>opposite</kanji> of measurement people. Which side are you on?
kanji.meaningHint: What's that, you say? It doesn't always have to be writing types versus measurement types? We can work together to create a better society? Nah, sorry, I'd rather it be me versus the world.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Whenever it's you <kanji>versus</kanji> someone else, you wear a <reading>tie</reading> (たい). Naturally, your tie is always the <kanji>opposite</kanji> color of your opponent's tie. Kinda like how political rivals wear different color ties when they debate. It's pretty silly, but at least your tie makes it clear that it's you versus them.
kanji.readingHint: Think of someone you know who's your total opposite. Now imagine you're both in ties, but opposite colors, and you're debating… or fighting in a cage match or something.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Your nation's <radical>flag</radical> sits on top of a <radical>cape</radical>d <radical>mouth</radical>. This is the symbol for the "<kanji>Bureau</kanji> of Secret Things." It's a special <kanji>department</kanji> of your government made to keep things hidden.
kanji.meaningHint: The cape covering the mouth represents how this bureau never talks about their secrets. The flag represents your country. Think about all the cool secret things the Bureau of Secret Things must have.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>bureau</kanji>'s best-kept secret is cloaking devices that <reading>cloak you</reading> (きょく) with the press of a button.
kanji.readingHint: Now, this mnemonic isn’t perfectly close, but the goal is to get you close enough in your brain so that you can remember きょく later. If you can get to CLOAK YOU, then you can get to きょく much easier than just trying to get there from scratch. So imagine working in this bureau and getting to cloak yourself all the time.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You <radical>loiter</radical> around with a <radical>weapon</radical> because you're currently doing your <kanji>service</kanji> and <kanji>duty</kanji> to your country. You're standing guard outside, waiting just in case something will happen.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine standing around with a weapon in your hands. It feels more like you're doing nothing, loitering around the wall, but this is how you offer your service to your country, so you have to do it.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You're about halfway through your <kanji>service</kanji>, when a <reading>yak</reading> (やく) walks by. It stops directly in front of you and grunts. "Excuse me, Mr. Yak, but it's my <kanji>duty</kanji> to escort you away from my country."
kanji.readingHint: Somehow your duty has become pushing this stubborn, hairy yak away from the entrance to your country. You poke it in the butt with your weapon, but it doesn't seem to care.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: In your <radical>fingers</radical> is a <radical>weapon</radical>, so you <kanji>throw</kanji> it. Maybe you're angry and you threw the weapon at a person you don't like. Maybe you're a pacifist and you threw it away so no one else could use it. Either way, when you have a weapon in your fingers you have to throw it.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a weapon in between your fingers. It doesn't matter what kind. Now feel the weight as you throw it.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You <kanji>throw</kanji> your weapon away because you're about to enter <reading>とう</reading>きょう and there are no weapons allowed there. There is, however, a big pile of thrown away weapons by the border, which is where you're throwing yours right now.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine throwing the weapon in your fingers just before you walk into とうきょう. You can see the lights, smell the smells! Throw your weapons and your cares away!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have at your disposal a <radical>tsunami</radical> to assassinate this <radical>person</radical>, or a <radical>hook</radical>. Which method will you choose? <kanji>Decide</kanji> now!
kanji.meaningHint: Have trouble with the decision. Which one? Tsunami will be big and cool, but a hook will be more discreet. How can you decide? Can you think of a neat way to decide this? You're like Two-Face deciding on how to kill Batman.
kanji.readingMnemonic:
To remember the けつ reading, we always use the word "ketsup." It's a special mix of ketchup and catsup (yum):

You finally <kanji>decide</kanji>. You're going to go with the tsunami... but not just any tsunami. You'll kill him with a tsunami of <reading>ketsu</reading>p (けつ).
kanji.readingHint: Get everything ready to take your target down. How will you collect enough ketsup to make a ketsup tsunami? Where will you unleash it? You gotta decide on the ketsup logistics now.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You dig a <radical>hole</radical> <radical>nine</radical> times for your <kanji>research</kanji>. You should always do research with nine variables so you can compare them, and so there's an uneven number.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine carefully digging a hole nine times, in nine different spots, so you can do your research. Hmm, I wonder what kind of research these holes are for…
kanji.readingMnemonic: Your <kanji>research</kanji> is on <reading>cu</reading>cumbers (きゅう)!
kanji.readingHint: Put nine full-grown cucumbers into their holes so you can research what happens next.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: When your <radical>self</radical> goes down a <radical>slide</radical> and hits a <radical>barb</radical>, it's a painful reminder that you have a <kanji>body</kanji>. Sometimes people think their self is just some kind of floating, disembodied consciousness, but getting a barb stuck in <kanji>oneself</kanji> while going down a slide will quickly remind one of one's bodily existence.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine hurtling down a slide, your inner self reveling in the joy of the moment. Then, you hit a sharp barb — OUCH!!! Suddenly, you're very conscious of your body again.
kanji.readingMnemonic: What part of your <kanji>body</kanji> did the barb get stuck in? Your <reading>shin</reading> (しん). That pointy little barb dug deep into your shin and made you painfully aware of the fact that <kanji>oneself</kanji> and one's body are inextricable.
kanji.readingHint: Feel the sharp pain in your shin as it radiates through your body. It kinda sucks, but in a way it's reassuring proof of the physical existence of oneself.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical and the kanji are exactly the same, so this means <kanji>someone</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Well, well… someone's lucky to not have to learn a new kanji.
kanji.readingMnemonic: If you don't know who <kanji>someone</kanji> is, odds are they're a <reading>sha</reading>man (しゃ). Only a shaman would have the mystical powers to obscure their own identity and pass themselves off as a mysterious, unknown "someone."
kanji.readingHint: Think back on someone you met recently whose name or face you can't really remember. Hate to break it to you, but… they were a shaman.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>stone</radical> <radical>lantern</radical> is an excellent way to <kanji>sharpen</kanji> anything, even in the dark. Your knives, your forks, your spoons, and even your sword.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine walking around at night and you need to sharpen your sword. You walk up to a stone lantern and rub your sword all over it to sharpen it. Touch the blade. Indeed, it's been sharpened!
kanji.readingMnemonic: Why did you <kanji>sharpen</kanji> your blade? Because you are about to do battle with <reading>Ken</reading> (けん), the famous samurai warrior.
kanji.readingHint:
You'll want to remember this character, because he will come up many times throughout your WaniKani journey. Ken the samurai used to work for WaniKani, but then he went rogue because he thought WaniKani wasn't being radical enough. So now he wanders the website carrying his squid friend (who you'll meet later) in a bucket.

To help you visualize him, imagine a samurai with armor made from crab shells, a helmet that is just an alligator head, and swords with crab claw hand guards. His great beard and mustache are styled in the shape of whatever kanji is giving you the most trouble at the time.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>horse</radical> radical and the <kanji>horse</kanji> kanji are exactly the same! Huzzah!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You are looking at a horse. It's looking at you. You try making horse noises at it, to get a reaction. Instead of reacting with a normal horse noise, it just makes sheep noises: "<reading>Baaa</reading>," (ば) it says. "Baaaaa."
kanji.readingHint: Feel the shock of this. It sounds just like a sheep, it's strange.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: This kanji is just the <radical>tree</radical> radical three times. Just based off this, you should be able to figure it out. This kanji means "<kanji>forest</kanji>."
kanji.meaningHint: Makes sense, because a bunch of individual trees is what makes up a forest!
kanji.readingMnemonic: One tree? No. Two trees? Not enough. I want <reading>more</reading> (もり) trees, please!
kanji.readingHint: Keep repeating this pattern over and over, continually focusing in on how you need "more" trees to make this forest. For some reason the person working with you only goes up by one at a time, though, so you have to say it a lot (it'll help you to remember, anyways!).

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Dirt</radical> makes it <radical>easy</radical> to identify your <kanji>location</kanji>. Even if you add an extra line to mark the ground, it's still easy. Keep that in mind and you can go from <kanji>place</kanji> to place.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine looking at the dirt. It's a distinct color and texture, and you're able to identify your location just from that alone. Now draw that line on the ground and you'll always remember this place.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Knowing your <kanji>location</kanji> from dirt is quite a feat! Who taught you that? It was <reading>Joe</reading> (じょう), the big local farmhand. Despite being a bit weird, he can identify any <kanji>place</kanji> just from its dirt!
kanji.readingHint: Remember Joe? He's our local farmhand who only has nine toes (from the 上 mnemonic). Imagine that guy explaining to you how to know your location from dirt. He may be a bit clumsy, but the man really knows his dirt.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>cross</radical> sticking out the top of the <radical>sun</radical> and another <radical>cross</radical> sticking out the bottom. The <radical>moon</radical> is off to the right. That's because it's the <kanji>morning</kanji>, which is when the sun and moon switch over. Those crosses are making sure the sun stays high in the sky for the rest of the day.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a sun attached up in the sky with two crosses, which act as scaffolding, and the moon gradually fading off to the right as the morning wears on.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Every <kanji>morning</kanji> you have <reading>Asa</reading>hi (あさ) beer for breakfast.
kanji.readingHint: You watch the sun scaffolded by crosses, and the moon next to it, as you sip on your early-morning Asahi.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have to <radical>sickle</radical> the <radical>rice paddy</radical> today because it's your <kanji>turn</kanji>. This kanji also means <kanji>number in a series</kanji>, which is a lot like a turn. For example, you're number 3, so your turn will be number 3.
kanji.meaningHint:
Go through in your mind the system your farm / village uses for deciding who has to sickle on any given day. It rotates, and it's a turn-based system. So, do you all stand in a line? Is there a calendar? Come up with something interesting, focusing on your turn in the process you come up with. 

 It will be helpful to remember both the "number in a series" and "turn" meanings for the vocab coming up in the future.
kanji.readingMnemonic: This <kanji>turn</kanji>-based rice sickle system is a contest as well! But, you are disappointed to find out that you have been <reading>ban</reading>ned (ばん) from the game because of the performance enhancing steroids you've been taking.
kanji.readingHint: Try to feel disappointed by this. Strange thing to feel disappointed by, but you were a great sickler. You were going to win the great prize, too (come up with something huge!), but now you're banned for the season.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: "Does the <radical>bamboo</radical> shirt <radical>suit</radical> me?" you ask... but nobody will <kanji>answer</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Shout "PLEASE ANSWER ME!" a few times to get the idea of "answer" in your head. What you really want is an answer, whether it's bad or good, but nobody's willing to say anything because you look so terrible.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You pull out a <reading>quarter</reading> (こた) and offer it to whoever will give you an <kanji>answer</kanji>.
kanji.readingHint: With this shiny quarter in your hand, everyone is giving you their answer. Yay for bribery!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: When a bunch of <radical>thread</radical>s are <radical>meet</radical>ing on paper (after you've dipped them in paint, say) they can create a masterpiece of a <kanji>picture</kanji> (or <kanji>painting</kanji>).
kanji.meaningHint: It's unbelievable the kind of picture you're able to paint with just the tips of threads. So much detail. So artistic. If it helps, imagine that you drew the Mona Lisa, better than the original, only using this thread tool.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You tell someone you painted this masterpiece of a <kanji>picture</kanji>. Their response? "<reading>EH</reading> (え)?!"
kanji.readingHint: Tell a few more people about your picture. Have them all do the same surprised "Eh?!" reaction at your art skills.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Here's a <radical>net</radical> full of of <radical>shellfish</radical> that you can <kanji>buy</kanji>. You can't just buy loose shellfish. You can only buy the ones that are in the net, bagged up and ready for your money.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine looking over a bunch of different kinds of shellfish wrapped in nets. Think about which ones you want to buy.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You decide to <kanji>buy</kanji> as many shellfish as you can fit in your <reading>ca</reading>r (か). You keep buying until your car is completely full of shellfish before you stop. Cars are totally a realistic unit of measure.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine buying an entire car's worth of shellfish. Mmm, delicious.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Aim the <radical>scooter</radical>'s <radical>neck</radical> at the <kanji>road</kanji>! Scooters are only meant for driving on <kanji>street</kanji>s and <kanji>path</kanji>s, and if you go the wrong <kanji>way</kanji>, you'll probably break your own neck!
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine riding your scooter down the road. You're carefully aiming the scooter's neck the right way so you don't end up going out of control and dying.
kanji.readingMnemonic:
To remember the reading どう we use the word "doughnut."

You're traveling down this <kanji>road</kanji> so fast that you don't see the giant <reading>dou</reading>ghnut (どう) that's rolling toward you until the last minute. You crash into it, and both you and the doughnut go tumbling down. Ahg, your neck!
kanji.readingHint: Alternate ending: You do a sweet jump, go right through the doughnut hole, take a bite, and land safely back onto the road!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>gate</radical> that the <radical>sun</radical> goes through at a regular <kanji>interval</kanji>. There is an <kanji>interval of time</kanji> in the sense that the sun goes through it at the same time every day. And there is an <kanji>interval of space</kanji> in the sense that it has to go through the space between the gate posts.
kanji.meaningHint: "Interval" is a weird word to remember, but just think of the sun going around the earth and through the gate like clockwork. Every 24 hours it passes through the gate, and each interval is exactly the same.
kanji.readingMnemonic:
This method of keeping track of <kanji>interval</kanji>s of time was invented by the great Khans of Mongolia, specifically the most famous Khan of all: Genghis <reading>Khan</reading> (かん).

Genghis Khan has had a huge impact on the world as we know it, especially the Eurasian continent of the past, so he's going to come up a lot from now on. Be prepared to get very familiar with him and his friends!
kanji.readingHint: Picture Genghis Khan ordering his most skilled inventors and builders to create this special sun gate so they can harness the power of intervals, and all people under his rule can benefit from the accurate telling of time.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>rain</radical> <radical>cloud</radical> is still a <kanji>cloud</kanji>! It's probably going to rain on you soon though, so I hope you have a jacket or an umbrella.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture all of the different types of clouds in the sky. There are puffy white ones, heavy dark ones, and wispy thin ones. But they're all clouds.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You lie down and try to figure out what the <kanji>cloud</kanji>s are shaped like. The first cloud is shaped... like a <reading>coo</reading>l <reading>mo</reading>m (くも). She's wearing high pants, and holding a kid on each hip, but she's also listening to the latest music and using slang. Huh. You look to the next cloud and see... wait, another cool mom?
kanji.readingHint: You look at each cloud and each one is a different cool mom. They're each doing different cool mom things. You suddenly don't want to look at the clouds anymore.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Give <radical>rice</radical> to a <radical>woman</radical> in <radical>winter</radical> so she can <kanji>count</kanji> it. The woman will count each individual grain of rice, then tell you the <kanji>amount</kanji> or <kanji>number</kanji> of grains.
kanji.meaningHint: She has to count each grain in order to divvy up the rice supply and make it last the winter. Imagine the amount you get today — just a small number of grains. It's not a good time for you guys…
kanji.readingMnemonic: The rice this woman has to <kanji>count</kanji> is for your <reading>sou</reading>p (すう). It's important to ration! You may not be getting many grains — few enough to count on two hands, probably — but at least you can enjoy them in a nice, hot bowl of soup.
kanji.readingHint: To remember that this is すう and not す, imagine the woman saying "soup" in a really drawn-out way, like "sooooouuuup." Try counting how many seconds it takes her to say it.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>white</radical> <radical>ice</radical> <radical>tree</radical> is a magical tree that radiates an aura of <kanji>comfort</kanji>, <kanji>ease</kanji>, and <kanji>pleasure</kanji>, with its icy foliage tinkling like beautiful <kanji>music</kanji> whenever it sways in the breeze.
kanji.meaningHint: Close your eyes and feel the aura of comfort wash over you. Listen to the musical tinkling of the tree's icy branches, setting you at ease. You never want this pleasurable moment to end!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You want more of this aura of <kanji>comfort</kanji>, so you chop down the magic tree and build a clothing <reading>rack</reading> (らく) out of it. Then, you put the rack in your house so you can enjoy that fuzzy feeling of comfort and ease every time you go to hang something up.
kanji.readingHint: Place a hanger on the rack. Feel the wave of pleasure that runs through you, and then bask in the afterglow of comfort and ease that it leaves behind. Now, go find something else to hang up on your rack. You need another hit of comfort and pleasure.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Say</radical> it with your <radical>tongue</radical>. If you do, you'll be able to <kanji>talk</kanji>. You'll be able to <kanji>speak</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Your problem is you weren't saying it with your tongue before. Once you start using your tongue, you're able to speak suddenly!
kanji.readingMnemonic: If something uses their tongue, it will be able to <kanji>talk</kanji> and <kanji>speak</kanji>. To prove this, you teach a <reading>wa</reading>lrus (わ) to use its tongue, and lo and behold, it speaks to you!
kanji.readingHint: You decided to teach a walrus how to speak because it seemed like the hardest thing to teach, with its tusks and all that. It turned out to be really easy. Although, you may have picked the Justin Long walrus, by accident. Either way, this walrus can speak! And you definitely (probably) helped.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You're in the <radical>rain</radical>, in a <radical>rice paddy</radical>, holding an <radical>umbrella</radical>. You're here because there's nothing else that's very tall around you. You want to get hit by <kanji>electricity</kanji> (aka lightning), to prove that it exists.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine being hit by the electricity. Feel the powerful electric shock pulse through your body. You're like a crazier Ben Franklin out here.
kanji.readingMnemonic: After the <kanji>electricity</kanji> hits you, you feel your face. In it is a huge <reading>den</reading>t (でん).
kanji.readingHint: Feel the indent in your face. It doesn't hurt, strangely, but it is pretty huge. Panic about this dent a bit.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You're tearing this <radical>door</radical> down with an <radical>axe</radical>. You're absolutely crazy. "I HATE THIS <kanji>PLACE</kanji>!!" you keep yelling as you smash in the door.
kanji.meaningHint: Why do you hate this place, in particular? Come up with a great reason why to help you to remember this very broad kanji meaning.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You smash through the door and finally get inside the <kanji>place</kanji>, only to find some kind of <reading>sho</reading>w (しょ) going on. It's a circus show — elephants, tightrope walkers, bears on unicycles! The greatest show on earth, but why is it at this place?
kanji.readingHint: Come up with a weird reason as to why the circus is at this place you hate so much. Why did you come here with your axe? Does it have something to do with the circus show?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Under a <radical>cliff</radical> there's a <radical>stool</radical>. If someone has a stool deep inside a cliff, they are most likely pretty <kanji>anti</kanji>-society, hiding away like that.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine someone who looks super anti-social (and a little feral). Ask them why they're sitting on this stool inside a cliff. They reply it's because they hate people. They're anti-people. In fact, they're anti-everything.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Turns out, when you go to this guy and pull off his beard, its the <kanji>anti</kanji>-hero from Star Wars, <reading>Han</reading> (はん) Solo! What is Han doing here, so hidden away? He's obviously hiding from Jabba because he doesn't want to get frozen in carbonite again.
kanji.readingHint: Make sure you get to the point where you pull this anti-social guy's beard off, to reveal Han Solo beneath. Be surprised... not just because he's Han Solo, but because he's real, too! Maybe you can yell out "Han! Your people need you!"

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word is made up of a single kanji with hiragana attached to it. That hiragana ends with い which means it's an adjective. So, what's the adjective form of the kanji that's in this word? 円 means both "yen" and "round" but in this case we're looking at the round one (because something isn't going to be "yenny"). The adjective version of round is <vocabulary>round</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>circular</vocabulary>. Just like a yen coin, this "round" is a flat round. As in, if you draw a circle on a piece of paper, you could use this word. Same goes with yen, which is why "yen" and "round" both use the same kanji.

So, if you know that the reading of 丸 is まる then you'll also know that the reading for this word is <reading>まる</reading>!

This verb is transitive, so you're doing the action to something. You're distinguishing between things or people.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: You should know the reading of 見 already. The second part, 分ける is a word you should have learned in the previous level. Combine that knowledge together and you get the reading for this word.

Turkish cuisine, Lebanese cuisine, Persian cuisine — you name it, とうきょう's got it.

vocabulary.readingMnemonic:

This word is commonly found in formal or professional contexts. In more casual settings, you can just use アドバイス (advise) instead.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>study</kanji> of <kanji>medicine</kanji> is <vocabulary>medical science</vocabulary>. It can also be called <vocabulary>medicine</vocabulary>, but make sure to think of it as the "medicine" where it has to do with "medical science."
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Okay, so the kanji itself means <kanji>buddy</kanji> and so does the word, but it also means <vocabulary>you</vocabulary> as well. This is one of the several ways to say "you" in Japanese, and this one is kind of an "affectionate" you. Maybe you'd say it with someone you're close to. Maybe you'd say it with a girlfriend or boyfriend. You wouldn't want to use it with your boss or teacher, though. Make sure to keep that in mind. It's kind of like saying "hey buddy" or "hey you," after all.

Who's your <vocabulary>buddy</vocabulary>? It's <reading>Kimmy</reading> (きみ)! If you know a Kimmy, imagine her. If you don't, find a famous Kimmy or make up a Kimmy to imagine. You ask... is it you?? Wait, you're my buddy?

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Add this to the end of someone's name, it's like saying ______<kanji>buddy</kanji>. It's generally used as a name ender (like さん) for boys and young men. Don't use this on people who are higher ranked than you (socially or literally). As in, you wouldn't use it on your boss. Use it on your younger male subordinates as well as boys who aren't adults yet.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji (on'yomi), probably because it usually is attached to other words (aka names, like こういち君) making it act more like jukugo words do.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
When you do (する) <kanji>versus</kanji>, you choose <vocabulary>to face</vocabulary> an opponent. It’s where your attention and efforts are going to <vocabulary>be directed toward</vocabulary>. Alternatively, you can use this word <vocabulary>to contrast</vocabulary> one thing with another.

This word is used to help point out the relationship between two things in a sentence, where one thing is focusing on another thing. This is all a little vague and perhaps confusing, so check out the collocations and context sentences to get a better grasp of this word!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji, so you should be able to read this word no problem.

In this case, the anti-versus of something would be the <vocabulary>opposite</vocabulary>. 

反対 refers to something that's opposite in direction, position, or nature. In some cases, it can also mean <vocabulary>opposition</vocabulary> because disagreeing or resisting to something means someone is taking the opposite side on a matter.

You can remember this because time feels longer in <reading>Ida</reading>ho (あいだ). Any interval of time you spend there feels so long, because Idaho life moves so slowly. <vocabulary>Over there</vocabulary>, a cow is saying <reading>moo</reading> (む). It's way over there, though, so you can't see or hear it. Kinda makes you wonder: if a cow moos way over there and no one's around to listen, did it really moo at all?

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Do you remember how 米国 can mean "America?" That 米 means America sometimes. So, when you see <kanji>all</kanji> <kanji>rice</kanji> (I mean, <kanji>America</kanji>), you can think of this word as meaning <vocabulary>All America</vocabulary> (sort of like how 全日本 means "All Japan.").
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Do you remember the word 思う? It means "to think." What you are <kanji>think</kanji>ing is <kanji>exit</kanji>ing—it's coming out of your head! You're recalling <vocabulary>a memory</vocabulary> or multiple <vocabulary>memories</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings are both kun'yomi, but based off of previous experience with the two separate words that make up this word, you should be able to read it. Just remember that it's kun'yomi. One hint is the hiragana sticking out of the 思.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Because this word ends with an う sound, you can tell it's probably a verb. The kanji portion means <kanji>near</kanji>. The verb version of that is <vocabulary>to draw near</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to get close</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to approach</vocabulary>. Essentially, the general idea is that you're getting closer to something. You're becoming more nearby. You're approaching.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: There's hiragana attached to this kanji, which means it's probably the kun'yomi reading (and it is). You've seen the kun'yomi reading via the word 近い. So, as long as you know that word, you should be able to read this one as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You know that 思う means "to think" and 出す means "to take out." So this is what happens when your brain takes a moment to think and pulls a memory out of storage. It means <vocabulary>to remember</vocabulary>!

You can shout 思い出した！when you recall your keys are in the fridge. (Again?!) You can also say 母を思い出します when something reminds you of your mom. In Japanese, you usually omit what reminded you of the memory because the important thing is the memory itself, filling your heart with touchy-feelies. Oh, mama!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the kun'yomi readings. You should know the words 思う and 出す and their readings, so you should be able to read this word if you know those words.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You've seen that 代わる means "to substitute for" or "to replace." This is the noun version of that (no う sound on the end). So, what is the noun version of those verb words? It would be <vocabulary>substitute</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>replacement</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: You should be able to figure out the reading from learning 代わる in the previous level.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This is the adverb version of the kanji <kanji>all</kanji>. So, it's like you add an 'ly' to it. But, that doesn't work too well (allly? c'mon). So, instead think of this word as <vocabulary>completely</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>entirely</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>truly</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

The person who <vocabulary>completely</vocabulary> doesn't understand this vocab word is <reading>Matt</reading> (まった). Be sure to take note of the small っ, too.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You know the word 長い from a couple levels ago. This is like the word 大きい versus 大きさ, where 大きさ is "size" and 大きい is "big." So, 長い is "long" and 長さ is <vocabulary>length</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: If you know the reading of the word 長い from level 6 you'll know the reading for this word too. Only difference is the さ at the end, which is hiragana so it should be easy to read.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: この means "this", and you know what the word 前  means (front/before). The combination of these words, "this before" if you will, can mean a few different things. If we're talking about when something happened, the "before" meaning kicks in, and it means <vocabulary>the other day</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>recently</vocabulary>. If we're talking about location, then the "front" meaning kicks in, and it means <vocabulary>in front of this</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for 前 is the kun'yomi, like the reading for the vocabulary word 前. So long as you know that word, you'll be able to read this one too. The reason it's not on'yomi is because it's like two words put together. The word この and the word 前.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This is a strange word, so you'll have to bear with me. You know that 知 means <kanji>know</kanji>. But in the case of this word, what do you know? Look at the second half. らせ sounds a bit like "race." So, you know about a "race." How do you know about this race? You got a <vocabulary>notice</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>notification</vocabulary> about it.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already with the kanji, so you should be all set. Lucky you!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Your <kanji>name</kanji> that's in the <kanji>front</kanji>. That is not your last name, that is your regular <vocabulary>name</vocabulary> or your <vocabulary>first name</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word uses both kun'yomi readings (oh darn!). That being said, you've seen the kun'yomi readings for both the kanji that make up this word. The word 名 (な) and the word 前 (まえ) both are kun'yomi, so use those words and Voltron them into a single word, なまえ.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You've seen the word 出来る (to be able to do), which is the first part. Then the second part, 上がる means "to rise." So, think about it this way: once you're able to do something, you rise because you're finished. That's why this verb means <vocabulary>to be finished</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is a combination of the readings from 出来る and 上がる. So long as you were paying attention in lessons past, you should be able to read this word as well just by combining those other words.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This is a verb because it ends with an う sound. What does the kanji mean? It's <kanji>music</kanji> and <kanji>bend</kanji>. In the case of this word, we're going with the "bend" version. The verb of that is <vocabulary>to bend</vocabulary>. This is when you're doing the bending. You can remember this because げ kind of looks like the <reading>ge</reading>cko you're bending. That gecko looked good before you bent him in half.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: How were you able <vocabulary>to bend</vocabulary> this gecko? Solo effort? No way! It actually took both you and your <reading>ma</reading>ma (ま) to make it happen! Just imagine you and your mighty mama, tag-teaming to bend a gecko in half!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You know that 交ぜる means <vocabulary>to mix</vocabulary> and that the kanji means <kanji>mix</kanji> as well. So, this probably has something to do with mixing things. This word means <vocabulary>to be mixed</vocabulary>. This is when something is mixed but it's not mixed by you. It's just being mixed. Think of it this way - the じ in 交じる is Jesus, who just uses Jesus magic to mix something. So, you're not mixing it. It's just when something is <vocabulary>to be mixed</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as with 交ぜる. So long as you know the ま portion of that word's reading, you'll be able to read this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You've seen the words 走る (to run) and 回る (to revolve). So, when you're running and revolving while you're doing it, you're running in circles. So, the verb form of that is <vocabulary>to run around</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings are those like the words 走る and 回る. Make sure you know those words from before and apply that knowledge to read this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You know that the kanji 当 means <kanji>right</kanji> or <kanji>success</kanji>. So since this is a verb, you're doing right and success (which doesn't make much sense). Instead, you're guessing something and getting it right. So, this word means <vocabulary>to guess</vocabulary> something. Hopefully you don't have to guess too hard when it comes to the meaning of this word as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading can be remembered via the word 当たる which you learned a few levels ago. Use that knowledge to remember that this word is read as あてる. The important part is the あ.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>change</kanji> so you'd think the verb version is "to change," but it's a bit more specific. This word means <vocabulary>to change form</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to transform</vocabulary>.

化ける means to change into something else, usually in a surprising and magical way. It's often used in stories where animals or spirits take on human forms. It can also describe transformations in real life that are so dramatic they feel unreal.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You try to transform. You want to turn into something awesome, like a dinosaur, but then *poof* you turn into a sheep. "<reading>Ba</reading>aaa," you say. "Baaa."

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You've already learned 回る, which means "to revolve" or "to rotate," and this is the transitive version of that. You're doing the turning/rotating action on something else, so this means <vocabulary>to turn something</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>to rotate something</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to spin something</vocabulary>.

To remember the difference, just think about how you might get <reading>sue</reading>d (す) if you started aggressively spinning one of those playground spinners while someone else's kids were playing on it. Pretty shady behavior.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the word 回る (まわ). So long as you know that word, you'll be able to read this one as well. Use both of these words together to remember their readings.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>I</kanji> am talking about my <kanji>self</kanji>, my own <kanji>body</kanji>… In other words, this is about me <vocabulary>personally</vocabulary> or what I <vocabulary>myself</vocabulary> have done.

私自身 literally means "I myself," and it's used to emphasize your personal involvement in something. For example, you may say 私自身の考え to highlight that something is your own thought, or 私自身から言う, to really stress that you'll personally be the one to say something to someone, without going through any intermediaries.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings are a bit weird here. The 私 is わたし, but the 自 and 身 use the readings you learned with the kanji. Just imagine the 私 saying to the other two, "I myself will use my vocab reading, but you two should use your kanji readings — got it?"

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You've seen 私立, which is "private," and you've seen 大学, which is "college" or "university." So, combine them together and you have a <vocabulary>private college</vocabulary> / <vocabulary>private university</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: If you know the readings of the words 私立 and 大学 you'll be able to read this. It's also all jukugo on'yomi readings too, so you can read it that way.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>before</kanji> <kanji>time</kanji> was <vocabulary>last time</vocabulary> or the <vocabulary>previous time</vocabulary>
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the vocab word are the same, so this means <vocabulary>body</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>oneself</vocabulary>. It also refers to <vocabulary>animal flesh</vocabulary> sometimes, meaning the non-bone edible parts of animals, including seafood. It's the "mi" in sashimi!

Wondering about the difference between 体 and 身? Basically, 体 is for the physical human (or animal) body as a whole, and is often used in relation to its condition or appearance. 身 can refer to a physical human body too, but unlike 体, it's also used to refer to the self as an individual and, by extension, to one's social standing or circumstances.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it probably uses the kun'yomi reading. You did not learn this reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember: 

Who does this <vocabulary>body</vocabulary> belong to? To <reading>me</reading> (み)!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember 地下, which is "below ground." Well, this is <kanji>ground</kanji> and <kanji>above</kanji> combined together, so I bet you can guess that this means <vocabulary>above ground</vocabulary>. But usually things above ground don't float (unless you're in space), so it's really <vocabulary>on the ground</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You know that 向く means "to face" or "to turn towards", and this verb is related. This is a transitive verb, meaning it takes a direct object. It's when someone turns or points something. That something doesn't just turn on its own. So this verb means <vocabulary>to turn something towards</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to point something at</vocabulary>.

In order to remember that this word means "to turn something towards," focus on the け. You have a bottle of ketchup in your hands and you're turning it toward your worst enemy to spray them. Picture yourself pointing the ketchup toward them.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this one is the same as 向く which you learned in a previous level. As long as you know that one you should be able to learn this one's reading as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The お is added to elevate someone in <kanji>front</kanji> of you. What do you call someone in front of you? That's right, <vocabulary>you</vocabulary>. Over time, this word has lost its sense of politeness, and nowadays it sounds very rough and often rude. This "you" is a good way to show anger, and some people also use it in very casual situations to show affection.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for 前 is the kun'yomi, like the reading for the vocabulary word 前. So long as you know that word, you'll be able to read this one too.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>Earth</kanji>'s <kanji>middle</kanji> <kanji>sea</kanji> is the <vocabulary>Mediterranean Sea</vocabulary>. You know, because it's surrounded by land. It's a sea in the middle of all that earth.

Actually, the Japanese name 地中海 matches the Latin roots of the English name too: medius for "middle" and terra for "earth." Whoa, did we just teach you some Latin? I sense a new business venture here. Wanius Kanius, anyone?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Every</kanji> <kanji>morning</kanji> is <vocabulary>every morning</vocabulary>!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is a combination of on'yomi and kun'yomi. That being said, both readings for both kanji are the readings you learned with the kanji so you should be able to read this.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You've seen how 当たり means success. If you've experienced success <kanji>before</kanji>, everything after that seems to be pretty <vocabulary>obvious</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>water</kanji> <kanji>road</kanji> carries your <vocabulary>water supply</vocabulary>. In the old days, these were called <vocabulary>aqueduct</vocabulary>s.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. 

The kanji itself means <kanji>point</kanji> so the verb version is something you need to point your finger to do. Picture pointing your finger and pushing a lightswitch <vocabulary>to turn something on</vocabulary>, in this case the light. You won't be able <vocabulary>to switch something on</vocabulary> if you can't point your finger.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You aren't able <vocabulary>to turn</vocabulary> the light on with just one finger though, you need to use <reading>two</reading> (つ). Either you have really weak fingers, or that's a really strong lightswitch. Either way, you need two fingers to switch on the light.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If you have an <kanji>eye</kanji> for <kanji>service</kanji>, then you'll always think helping people is your <vocabulary>duty</vocabulary>! If you see someone in need of service, you’ll always offer your help, because that’s your duty.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word consists of the on'yomi reading for 役 and the kun'yomi reading for 目. You've learned them both so you should be able to read this word too!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Life</kanji> that comes out of the <kanji>earth</kanji> is made up of different kinds of <vocabulary>material</vocabulary>s. Sometimes it's <vocabulary>cloth</vocabulary>, sometimes it's <vocabulary>dough</vocabulary>, but everything has to be made out of something.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This word uses a new kun'yomi reading for 生 and a new on'yomi reading for 地. You haven't learned either of these readings yet, sorry! Here's some mnemonics to help you:

If you want the best <vocabulary>material</vocabulary> to make clothes or pies out of, the <reading>key</reading> (き) is asking <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ)! He knows everything, including where to find the materials for whatever weird thing you're making. Just remember: Who's the key? Jesus!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Use a <kanji>number in a series</kanji> to <kanji>group</kanji> the things you watch and listen to. That makes them your <vocabulary>program</vocabulary>s. Your TV and radio programs, specifically. If you watch TV you'll hear it a lot!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word consists of the on'yomi reading for 番 and the kun'yomi reading for 組. You've learned them both so as long as you remember the rendaku, you should be able to read this word too!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If you've got an <kanji>eye</kanji> on a certain <kanji>course</kanji>, it's a <vocabulary>subject</vocabulary> you really want to take. Maybe you're in school and that means you'll be taking a lot of <vocabulary>course</vocabulary>s. Maybe you're a teacher and you're planning out your <vocabulary>curriculum</vocabulary>. Either way, you have your eye on the course-prize.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings are the on'yomi readings, but you learned the kun'yomi reading for 目 before. So, you have to remember that this word uses もく instead of め. To do that, imagine seeing that the <vocabulary>subjects</vocabulary> you're allowed to take next term are different than everyone else's. The other kids notice, and start <reading>mock</reading>ing (もく) you for it. Think of what those subjects are and how you're being mocked for having to take them.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When a <kanji>number</kanji> of <kanji>year</kanji>s have passed you say that <vocabulary>several years</vocabulary> have passed! You don't want to say how many years, so just say several years.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember how 文字 means "letter"? Well, these are the little <kanji>picture</kanji> letters people use to communicate these days, aka <vocabulary>emoji</vocabulary>. You know, the faces, hearts, and flames you send when you text or email — emoji!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a combination of the words 絵 and 文字, which you've learned already. If you can read those, you should be able to read this too.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You already know that 手 means "hand," but it can also mean "doer," as in someone who performs a particular action or task. Why? Because we use our hands to do things. And when it comes to <kanji>throw</kanji>ing, the <kanji>doer</kanji> is the <vocabulary>pitcher</vocabulary>!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 手 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

To be a good <vocabulary>pitcher</vocabulary>, all you have to do is put the ball into the <reading>chute</reading> (しゅ). Pitchers don't actually throw the ball. There is an invisible pitching chute right on the mound. You slide the ball into the chute and off it goes!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
When it's you <kanji>versus</kanji> someone else to <kanji>decide</kanji> it all, you know this is a <vocabulary>showdown</vocabulary>. It's a decisive <vocabulary>confrontation</vocabulary>!

対決 is when two sides go head-to-head in a serious match or showdown. Think rivals <vocabulary>facing off</vocabulary> in a big game or the final battle in an anime. It's tense and dramatic, but also exciting — like, "Alright, this is it. Time to settle things. Who's gonna come out on top?"
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This combines <kanji>south</kanji> and アフリカ, the word for "Africa." Put them together to get <vocabulary>South Africa</vocabulary>. 

南アフリカ will almost always mean the country of South Africa, but in some contexts it'll occasionally refer to the wider region of <vocabulary>Southern Africa</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading uses the kun'yomi for 南, which you've already learned. Yay for geography! Now which continent was South Africa on again…?

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
From the <kanji>north</kanji> comes a <kanji>wind</kanji>. Naturally, it's the <vocabulary>north wind</vocabulary>.

北風 blows down from the north, and in Japan is often associated with the colder temperatures it brings.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. Almost like it's two independent vocab words, 北 and 風, mashed together. You've learned these readings, but the かぜ reading is still pretty new, so here's a mnemonic just in case:

Imagine the <vocabulary>north wind</vocabulary> blowing a kami<reading>kaze</reading> (かぜ) off course. The kamikaze pilot tries to complete his mission, but he can't overcome the wind blowing down from the north. Hear the kamikaze crying out, "Curse you, north wind!" In a way though, it kind of saves his life.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
We have <kanji>night</kanji> and the noun version of "to dawn" (明ける). What comes when the night ends and a new day dawns? The <vocabulary>dawn</vocabulary>, of course.

夜明け refers to dawn or <vocabulary>daybreak</vocabulary> in the literal sense, but it can also be used metaphorically to mean the <vocabulary>beginning</vocabulary> of something new, as in 時代の夜明け (the dawn of an era).
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings of the kanji. You know 明け because it uses the same reading as 明ける, but 夜 is a little weird because よる gets shortened to よ. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember this change:

What are you doing when <vocabulary>dawn</vocabulary> comes each morning? Playing with your <reading>yo</reading>-yo (よ), obviously. You want to be the best yo-yoer there's ever been, so you're up with the dawn every morning, practicing your yo-yo skills while the competition sleeps.

Note that in the related phrase 夜が明ける, 夜 is also often read as よ.
